newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania's exiled king backs reforms.
newsitem.headline: Romania's exiled king backs reforms.

text.p: Romania's exiled King Michael, visiting his homeland after having his citizenship restored, told the Balkan country's prime minister on Saturday he backed his market reforms, a government statement said.

Michael was acclaimed by thousands of Romanians after arriving on Friday for a five-day visit officially described as private, though crowds have been considerably smaller than during his first homecoming in 1992.

The 75-year-old monarch, forced to abdicate by Communists in 1947, has promised to abide by Romania's 1991 constitution. His programme includes meetings with the country's new centrist leadership, which hopes to use his prestige to boost its longshot chances of early membership in an expanded NATO.
"I hope the Romanian people understand the necessity of facing up to difficulties," the statement said Michael told Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea at a lunch closed to reporters.

"If these matters are not tackled now, we will never solve our problems. Our affairs were in disarray during the war and afterwards. We must return to where Romania needs to be. Romania's membership of NATO is extremely important for us."
Ciorbea told the king the programme would "give Romania the place it deserves alongside the civilised countries of the world and allow it to enter NATO and the European Union".

Romania's government, which ousted ex-communists in last November's election, has undertaken to make up ground on what are generally viewed as serious delays in introducing market reforms after the 1989 fall of communism.
The programme, drawn up with international lenders, has already freed many prices and hit living standards of Romanians earning average monthly salaries equivalent to less than $100.
The King, who received a new Romanian passport on his arrival, repeated that his stay was "not a visit. I am returning to my homeland."
Michael is to attend a service on Sunday at the "Church of the Patriarchate", headquarters of the Romanian Orthodox church. He meets President Emil Constantinescu on Tuesday.
Opinion polls show only a small fraction of Romanians favour restoration of the monarchy, though one of two small monarchist parties is within the new ruling centrist coalition.

On his first return, Michael drew hundreds of thousands into the streets at Orthodox Easter. A later visit was blocked by ex-president Ion Iliescu, who treated him as a foreign commoner and insisted he publicly accept the constitution.
